doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: How they came to work with so many musicians
summary: Monk Rowe asks how they have worked with so many artists; both say friends recommend you, and a broad grounding in music helps.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we are filming at Hamilton College for the Jazz Archive. I’m very pleased to have two interesting personalities with me today, Adam Nussbaum and Dan Wall, who just described himself as a keyboard wizard. Is that what I heard correctly?
That would be an adequate description of him for sure.
There were other much better words than that, that I won’t repeat.

You know I’m looking at some of the information that was sent to me about you fellas and I think next time you do your resumes you could almost write down here’s the people I haven’t played with and you’d actually have a shorter list. It’s amazing to me how many musicians that you guys have worked with. How does that come about?

I think what happens is you get to New York, you have friends that you meet on the scene, they have maybe gigs and associations with people that are established, your name gets out there, people hear about you, friends recommend you, people hear you, and it kind of works that way. And being able to fulfill the requirements of jobs is one way to get another job. I mean a buddy of mine said the best way to get a gig is to have a gig. Because people hear you and then they can always find your number. And a lot of elements come into play. You know luck is I think when skill and opportunity meet.
All right, that’s a good description.

And I think that’s something I’ve been very fortunate to have. And I feel very blessed to have had the opportunities to play with so many great musicians, because it’s a constant learning process for me.
Um hum. Did it pretty much happen the same way for you, Dan?

Yeah, I think what Adam said is very true, that you know you meet people, you play with them, they like your playing or they don’t like your playing, but if they like your playing then they tell a friend of theirs about this person. Because they know that this person they’re speaking with would enjoy a certain thing that you do, certain interaction you have with people, and you connect with them and from them you connect with somebody else. And it’s, you know, hopefully you get a flow going out of it. And another thing

that’s probably important too to work with a lot of people is to have developed kind of a broad understanding of music, you know, roots, so that you’re, I mean you can look at someone who’s a specialist and they only do one thing, but if you look at the big picture of things I think that if you can be a diverse player then your chances are much better for getting out there and working with a lot of different people because everybody’s a little different.
